title: Max Points on a Line
pattern: normalized direction vectors hashed with GCD
statement:
You are given `points`, a list of rows. Each row describes one point: its first entry is the point's x coordinate and its second entry is its y coordinate. Only those first two entries are read, so any further entries in a row are ignored. A row holding fewer than two entries describes no point at all: it is skipped and never counts towards the answer.

Several rows may describe the same location; every row is a separate point and each one is counted separately.

Return the largest number of points that lie on one single straight line. The line may run in any direction, including vertical and horizontal, and a line is allowed to contain coincident points, each of which counts. With a single point the answer is 1, and when no row describes a point at all the answer is 0.

For example, with `[[1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3], [4, 5]]` the three points with equal coordinates sit on the line `y = x`, so the answer is 3. With `[[0, 0], [0, 0], [1, 1]]` the first two rows describe the same location and all three points lie on `y = x`, so the answer is 3.

Constraints: `1 <= points.length <= 200`, `1 <= points[i].length <= 200` and `-100 <= points[i][j] <= 100`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: A line is determined by one point on it plus a direction. Use each row that describes a point as an anchor and count how many other points lie in each direction away from it.
A row is a coordinate list, not a fixed pair: read its first two entries only, ignore anything beyond them, and skip a row that holds fewer than two entries instead of indexing past its end.
Compare directions exactly: divide each difference vector by the GCD of its components, fix the sign, and use that reduced pair as a map key. Floating-point slopes are not safe here.
Repeated coordinates have no direction from the anchor, so tally them separately and add the tally to the best direction group, because every copy sits on every line through that location.

editorial.approach: The brute force takes every pair of rows that describe a point and compares their two coordinates with a cross-product test, counting how many of the n rows are collinear with that pair and keeping the largest count. Rows are coordinate lists, not fixed pairs: only the first two entries are read, a row with fewer than two entries describes no point and is skipped everywhere, and a pair whose two rows describe the same location has no direction, so it is skipped as well, because the zero vector makes every cross product vanish and would inflate the count to n. A separate tally of the most repeated location covers inputs where every point coincides. The optimal version makes this O(n^2): for each anchor point it reduces the vector to every later point by the GCD of its components, fixes the sign of the reduced pair, and groups reduced pairs in a hash map. The best line through the anchor is the largest group plus the number of entries sitting on the anchor's own location.
editorial.why_optimal: Every line holding at least two distinct locations is pinned down by any pair of its points, so anchoring each point and scanning only the points after it covers each line once, and O(n^2) is the natural floor for the pairwise comparison this problem forces. The hash map holds at most n - 1 keys, giving O(n) extra space. Integer reduction by GCD keeps the keys exact, which floating-point division cannot promise. Skipping short rows costs one length check per row and does not change the bound.
editorial.pitfalls: Indexing a row as if it always held exactly two entries: rows are coordinate lists of any length, so only the first two entries may be read and a shorter row has to be skipped rather than indexed, and the extra entries of a longer row must be ignored. Initialising the running best to 1, which reports one point for an input whose rows are all too short and so describes no point at all; the count starts at 0 and the empty case is exactly what that baseline is for. Comparing slopes as floating-point numbers: 1/3 and 2/6 describe the same direction but only become the same key after dividing both components by their GCD. Skipping the sign fix, so that (1, -2) and (-1, 2) fall into different buckets. Feeding coincident rows into the direction map even though they have no direction from the anchor, which double-counts them or corrupts a bucket. Mishandling vertical lines, where dx is 0 and only dy carries the sign; the sign rule must normalise that case too.
